question: A sample of 23.4 g of NaCl is used in the first-stage laboratory preparation of HCl. Assume complete reaction with excess concentrated H₂SO₄. Which set gives the moles of HCl formed, mass of NaHSO₄ formed and volume of HCl at STP, respectively?
explanation:

The first-stage equation produces 0.4 mol HCl and 0.4 mol NaHSO₄.

V(HCl)=0.4×22.4=8.96 L

title: Board-style Limiting reagent and gas volume
question: A mixture contains 13.0 g of Zn and 7.30 g of HCl. The reaction is Zn+2HCl→ ZnCl₂+H₂ What volume of hydrogen is produced at STP?
explanation:
n(Zn)=(13 / 65)=0.2 mol



n(HCl)=(7.30 / 36.5)=0.2 mol


Two moles of HCl are required per mole of Zn. HCl is therefore the limiting reagent.


n(H₂)=(0.2 / 2)=0.1 mol



V(H₂)=0.1×22.4=2.24 L


Option A incorrectly assumes that all 0.2 mol of Zn reacts.

title: Board-style A multi-step chloride test
question: An aqueous solution is treated with AgNO₃, producing a white curdy precipitate. The precipitate remains after dilute HNO₃ is added but dissolves when NH₄OH is added. A separate portion of the original solution gives a white precipitate with Pb(NO₃)₂ that dissolves on heating. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Both precipitates are AgCl, and both must dissolve in dilute HNO₃.
The first precipitate is PbCl₂ and the second is AgCl.
The observations are consistent with chloride ions: AgCl is insoluble in dilute HNO₃ but soluble in NH₄OH, while PbCl₂ dissolves on heating.
The first precipitate is Ag₂O and the second is PbO, proving that the solution contains no chloride ions.

explanation:
The two tests have distinct characteristic behaviours. AgNO₃ gives white curdy AgCl, insoluble in dilute HNO₃ and soluble in NH₄OH. Lead nitrate gives white PbCl₂, which dissolves on heating. The observations are consistent with chloride ions.

title: Board-style Integrated final challenge
question: A student prepares HCl by heating NaCl with concentrated H₂SO₄ below 200°C, dries the gas with concentrated H₂SO₄, collects it by upward delivery, and then dissolves a portion in water. The aqueous solution is tested with blue litmus and AgNO₃. Which sequence of conclusions is entirely correct?

options.text: Na₂SO₄ forms in the first stage; HCl is collected over water; dry blue litmus turns red; AgNO₃ gives a black precipitate.
NaHSO₄ forms in the first stage; HCl is lighter than air; aqueous blue litmus remains blue; AgCl dissolves in dilute HNO₃.
NaHSO₄ forms in the first stage; HCl is dried with quicklime; dry blue litmus turns red; AgNO₃ produces PbCl₂.

NaHSO₄ forms in the first stage; HCl is dried with concentrated H₂SO₄ and collected by upward delivery; dry blue litmus remains blue, aqueous blue litmus turns red, and AgNO₃ gives white curdy AgCl insoluble in dilute HNO₃.

explanation:
The first-stage reaction is


NaCl+H_2SO₄(conc.)→ NaHSO₄+HCl


Concentrated H₂SO₄ dries HCl, which is collected by upward delivery because it is heavier than air. Dry HCl does not turn dry blue litmus red, but aqueous HCl does. Silver nitrate produces white curdy AgCl, insoluble in dilute HNO₃. Option C uses an unsuitable drying agent and incorrectly predicts the litmus result.

title: Percentage purity of an impure NaCl sample
question: An impure 12.6 g sample containing NaCl is treated with excess concentrated H₂SO₄ below 200°C. The HCl obtained is collected as 4.48 L of dry gas at STP. Assuming the NaCl is the only source of HCl and the reaction proceeds completely, what is the percentage purity of the original sample?
explanation:
First calculate the moles of HCl:


n(HCl)=(4.48 / 22.4)=0.2 mol


From the first-stage equation, NaCl:HCl = 1:1.


n(NaCl)=0.2 mol


Mass of pure NaCl present:


m=0.2×58.5=11.7 g


Percentage purity:


begin{aligned}
% purity
&=(mass of pure NaCl / mass of impure sample)×100
&=(11.7 / 12.6)×100
&=92.86%
end{aligned}


Option B assumes the whole sample is pure NaCl, while option A incorrectly uses the mass of HCl as the mass of NaCl.

title: Limiting reagent in the second stage of laboratory preparation
question: At about 500°C, 24.0 g of sodium hydrogen sulphate (NaHSO₄) is heated with 8.775 g of sodium chloride (NaCl). The reaction is NaHSO₄+NaCl→ Na_2SO₄+HCl Assuming complete reaction of the limiting reagent, which result is correct?

options.text: 4.48 L HCl is formed, and 12.0 g NaHSO₄ remains.
3.36 L HCl is formed, 21.3 g Na₂SO₄ is formed, and 6.0 g NaHSO₄ remains.
2.24 L HCl is formed, and no NaHSO₄ remains.
3.36 L HCl is formed, 14.2 g Na₂SO₄ is formed, and no NaHSO₄ remains.

explanation:
Molar masses:


M(NaHSO₄)=120,quad M(NaCl)=58.5


Moles of reactants:


n(NaHSO₄)=(24 / 120)=0.2



n(NaCl)=(8.775 / 58.5)=0.15


The reaction ratio is 1:1, so NaCl is the limiting reagent.

HCl formed:


V=0.15×22.4=3.36 L


Na₂SO₄ formed:


m=0.15×142=21.3 g


NaHSO₄ remaining:


(0.2-0.15)×120=6.0 g


Option D incorrectly assumes all NaHSO₄ reacts despite insufficient NaCl.

---

title: Excess reactant in direct HCl synthesis
question: A mixture contains 8.0 g of H₂ and 71.0 g of Cl₂. They react according to H₂+Cl₂→2HCl Assuming complete reaction of the limiting reagent, what mass of H₂ remains unreacted and what mass of HCl is formed?

explanation:
Moles of hydrogen:


n(H₂)=(8.0 / 2)=4 mol


Moles of chlorine:


n(Cl₂)=(71 / 71)=1 mol


Cl₂ is the limiting reagent and consumes 1 mol H₂, which has a mass of 2 g.


m(H₂ remaining)=8-2=6 g


One mole of Cl₂ produces two moles of HCl:


m(HCl)=2×36.5=73.0 g


Option D incorrectly assumes that all 4 mol H₂ can react with just 1 mol Cl₂.

title: Board-style Integrated preparation and gas collection
question: A student heats 11.7 g of NaCl with excess concentrated H₂SO₄ below 200°C. The evolved HCl is passed through a drying bottle and collected at STP. Which combination is correct?

options.text: 2.24 L HCl; collected over water; Na₂SO₄ forms in the flask.
4.48 L HCl; dried with quicklime; collected by downward delivery because HCl is lighter than air.
4.48 L HCl; dried using concentrated H₂SO₄; collected by upward delivery; NaHSO₄ forms in the flask.
8.96 L HCl; dried using dilute H₂SO₄; collected by upward delivery; NaHSO₄ forms in the flask.

explanation:
n(NaCl)=(11.7 / 58.5)=0.2 mol


The first-stage equation gives a 1:1 ratio of NaCl to HCl.


V(HCl)=0.2×22.4=4.48 L


NaHSO₄ forms below 200°C. Concentrated H₂SO₄ dries HCl, and its greater density than air permits collection by upward delivery. Option B has the right volume but specifies an unsuitable drying agent and the wrong collection direction.

title: Board-style Industrial preparation and absorption
question: Hydrogen and chlorine combine directly to form HCl. If 5.6 L of H₂ reacts completely with 5.6 L of Cl₂ at the same temperature and pressure, what volume of HCl is formed before absorption into water?
explanation:
H₂+Cl₂→2HCl


The volume ratio at equal temperature and pressure is 1:1:2.


V(HCl)=2×5.6=11.2 L


Option A forgets that two volumes of HCl form from one volume each of hydrogen and chlorine.

title: Identifying an error in the absorption apparatus
question: (Image reference: Figure 5: Incorrect inverted-funnel arrangement)* What is the principal risk introduced by this incorrect arrangement?

options.text: HCl will become lighter than air and escape upwards through the funnel.
The dissolved HCl will change into dry hydrogen chloride gas.
The extreme solubility of HCl can cause back suction, allowing water to be drawn into the gas-generating apparatus.
The submerged funnel rim prevents HCl from contacting water, so no absorption can occur.

explanation:
Because HCl dissolves extremely rapidly, the pressure inside the gas-generating apparatus can fall and water may be sucked backwards. Keeping the funnel rim just touching the surface helps minimise this risk. Option D is incorrect because immersion does not prevent contact between HCl and water.
